items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: New York Association for Business Economics: 'Monetary Policy at a Crossroads'
items.quote: If we get another hot reading on core inflation this week, then the FOMC will need to consider tightening monetary policy in the near term.
items.summary: Core PCE has risen from 3.0% in December to 3.4% in May and the increase is broad; the labor market is stable so his focus is inflation. He would keep holding if core inflation shows several months of lower readings, but says the FOMC has to be ready to tighten to avoid repeating 2021-22, and that anchored expectations do not excuse inaction. Cautions that the labor market is less tight than in 2022, so overtightening risks recession.
items.score_note: Two-sided ('crossroads') but the weight is on being ready to hike in the near term and policy possibly being insufficient at its current setting; conditional on data, so +1.

items.speaker: Philip Jefferson
items.occasion: Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research (SIEPR), Stanford University: 'Navigating Economic Shocks: A Monetary Policymaker's Perspective'
items.quote: I believe that it could be appropriate to reconsider our current policy stance to ensure we fulfill our commitment to deliver price stability
items.summary: Says the June hold at 3.50-3.75% should let inflation resume falling and policy is 'well positioned', but if actual inflation does not start to cool soon it could be appropriate to reconsider the stance. Warns the quick succession of energy, tariff and AI shocks raises the risk that inflation becomes entrenched. Notes AI could raise r*, making a given funds rate more accommodative.
items.score_note: Base case is hold, but he explicitly opens the door to tightening if inflation does not cool soon and frames the main risk as entrenched inflation; conditional, so +1 not +2.

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: Reuters NEXT Newsmaker Interview, Washington: prepared opening remarks 'The Economic Outlook and Some Comments on My Policy Communication'
items.quote: If there is continued progress toward our 2 percent goal, then I am willing to support holding the policy rate at its current level.
items.summary: Says recent data finally show signs of disinflation (3-month core PCE down from 4.76% in February to 3.05% in July) and he is inclined to hold on September 15-16 if August inflation confirms it; if inflation comes in hot he would consider a hike, since policy is 'only slightly restricting' demand. Describes this as his reaction function, not forward guidance.
items.score_note: Explicitly conditional both ways with the base case a hold; torn between 0 and +1 (he says it would not take much to move him to hike), chose the level nearer 0. Markets cut September hike odds after the remarks.

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: Reuters NEXT Newsmaker Interview, Washington: moderated Q&A with Reuters (same event as the prepared remarks)
items.quote: Give disinflation a chance
items.summary: In the Q&A he urged patience: wait and see whether the next inflation report extends the improvement rather than hike prematurely, though not 'until next year'. AP separately quotes him from the same Reuters interview: willing to 'sit and wait and be patient', but if inflation reverses 'it's time to pull the trigger and hike rates' (https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/fed-governor-waller-muddies-outlook-on-possible-rate-hike-later-this-month).
items.score_note: Same occasion as the prepared remarks (Q&A portion), kept separate because the wording differs; patience is the lead message with a hike as the conditional alternative, so 0.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Atlantic Council Front Page event, Washington: moderated Q&A with Josh Lipsky (same event as the eSLR remarks)
items.quote: I think we need to see how the September increase makes its way through the economy before we decide what further action may need to be taken
items.summary: Asked about the October meeting, she said inflation remains above target but after the September hike the Committee needs a better read on underlying trends and financial conditions; she does not currently see an urgent need for further action. Asked whether that puts her apart from the SEP median of one more hike this year, she repeated that the September increase should work through the economy first.
items.score_note: Wait-and-see hold with inflation still acknowledged as above target; she does not oppose further hikes, so 0 rather than -1. Source is the host's AI-generated transcript ('check against delivery').

items.speaker: Philip Jefferson
items.occasion: Darden School of Business, University of Virginia: 'The U.S. Economy and Monetary Policy'
items.quote: My colleagues and I will need to come to our own judgment, which may take more time.
items.summary: Says he supported the September 25bp hike as an important step to keep longer-term inflation expectations anchored; inflation is too high, with risks to his inflation forecast tilted to the upside and activity/employment risks roughly balanced. On next steps he gives no commitment: yields have risen further since September, and judging whether inflation returns to target fast enough 'may take more time'. Dow Jones read it as a signal the Fed may wait until December or later.
items.score_note: Inflation risk dominates and he endorses the hike, so leaning tighter; but no call for a near-term follow-up hike and an explicit 'may take more time', so +1 not +2. Market read on the day was patience (October hike odds fell).

items.speaker: Philip Jefferson
items.occasion: Darden School of Business, University of Virginia: moderated conversation with Prof. Bo Sun after the speech (UVA write-up, published Oct 6)
items.quote: We have to be prepared to do the work necessary to validate those expectations.
items.summary: In the conversation after his speech he said longer-term inflation expectations are still consistent with 2%, which he reads as evidence of Fed credibility, but that he does not take that for granted and the Fed must be prepared to do the work to validate them. On AI and the neutral rate: sustained evidence of higher productivity growth would be persuasive, but 'it's too soon to say'.
items.score_note: Same occasion as the Darden speech (Q&A portion). Readiness to act to keep expectations anchored leans tighter, with no timing given; +1. items.occasion: Istanbul Economic Forum, Central Bank of the Republic of Turkiye: 'The Signaling Value of the Summary of Economic Projections'
items.quote: If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2 percent goal.
items.summary: Explains his September hike vote as a preponderance of evidence (stable labor market, persistent energy, AI-buildout and tariff price pressures) that the December-2025-to-September stance would not return inflation to 2% in a timely way. Anticipates additional hikes; they need not come at consecutive meetings but should be in place within an acceptable period. Notes 16 of 18 SEP participants saw at least one more hike in 2026 and that near-term policy is focused on inflation.
items.score_note: Says more hikes are needed and that he anticipates them; flexibility is only about timing (leaves room for an October pause).

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: Bank of England Watchers Conference, King's Business School, London: 'The Economic Outlook and Some Thoughts on Labor Market Dynamism'
items.quote: I would still support a 25 basis point increase in the FOMC's policy rate at our December meeting
items.summary: Says further tightening is needed 'sooner rather than later'. He held in October only because signaled hikes were already priced, and those hikes must be delivered. Would back a 25bp hike in December even if October CPI improves; if core CPI is again around 0.3% or higher, a 50bp hike should be considered because 25bp would put credibility at risk. September inflation was 'bad' and broad (over 70% of core services components above 3%). In later remarks the same morning (Newsquawk wrap, paraphrase with quoted fragments) he said that at a minimum the Fed needs to take back the three insurance cuts, but that he is not "super hawkish" and is not looking to tighten by 150-200bp (https://www.newsquawk.com/headlines/newsquawk-us-market-wrap---hawkish-waller-and-hot-cpi-ignite-fed-50bps-rate-hike-bets).
items.score_note: Explicit support for a December hike and conditional support for 50bp.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Council on Foreign Relations, C. Peter McColough Series, Washington: 'The U.S. Economy and Considerations for Monetary Policy'
items.quote: This indicates that there is still work to do to bring inflation closer to 2 percent.
items.summary: Supported the October hold to assess the September hike; now says inflation is more persistent than she expected and broadening (core PCE likely 3.3% in October), the labor market is firming, and she is more attentive to the inflation side. But financial conditions have tightened, so the benefit of additional tightening must be weighed against costs for rate-sensitive sectors, and she wants clarity on AI financing conditions; flags AI-related debt on track to exceed $800 billion and off-balance-sheet structures as a risk to activity and financial stability. Identical remarks were given the same day at an Unleash Prosperity Now virtual event (18:30 ET per the Fed index).
items.score_note: Inflation is the priority and 'there is still work to do', but she stops short of endorsing a December hike and stresses tightening costs and AI-financing risks; +1 not +2.
items.ai_quote: Greater clarity on AI-related financing conditions and the sustainability of AI investments should increase my confidence in future policy decisions.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Council on Foreign Relations, C. Peter McColough Series, Washington: moderated Q&A with John Lipsky and audience (same event as the speech)
items.quote: I gave an indication today that I think addressing inflation is the right move for us
items.summary: Said that with the labor market stabilized she is shifting her focus to inflation, which is not on a downward trend, and that this 'should give us some pause as we think about the need to address inflation, and at what pace, and on what timeline'. Asked by the WSJ about colleagues calling for faster tightening, she let their statements speak for themselves. Compared the path to last year's gradual cuts with a pause, 'in the same way that we may work to address inflation in the coming months'. Longer-term expectations are very well anchored but do not control her thinking; she needs AI-buildout and Middle East risks to abate before being confident in her 2027 disinflation forecast.
items.score_note: Clear lean toward tightening ('addressing inflation is the right move') but gradual and with no commitment on December size or timing; +1. Q&A portion of the same occasion as the prepared speech.

items.speaker: Philip Jefferson
items.occasion: University of California, San Diego Economic Roundtable: 'New Technology, Old Questions: Productivity Puzzles and the Macroeconomy'
items.quote: I see the trajectory of inflation as providing the more important signal for determining the appropriate stance of monetary policy
items.summary: Mostly about AI and productivity, then the outlook: he voted to hold in October; since then activity and labor market are broadly solid while inflation readings show persistent price pressures (PCE 3.6%, core 3.1% in September, October data still well above target). Says inflation trajectory is the more important signal for the stance; further adjustments depend on data. AI investment demand is pushing up resource utilization and prices now, with supply gains later.
items.score_note: Explicitly puts inflation ahead of employment as the signal for policy and describes persistent price pressures, but does not commit to a December hike; +1.

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: CNBC interview with Steve Liesman (reported by Reuters)
items.quote: then you have to go 50 in December
items.summary: Says inflation is 'heading in the wrong direction and it is spreading out' into services, and businesses are starting to treat 3% as normal, so the Fed needs aggressive action: either a 50bp hike on December 8-9 or a 25bp hike with a very clear signal (statement or press conference) of another hike in January. Per Stocktwits' account of the same interview he said last year's three 'insurance cuts' should be reversed, 'three hikes plus maybe some more', and that he sees no AI bubble but the Fed is examining banks' leveraged lending to AI firms (https://stocktwits.com/news-articles/markets/equity/fed-s-waller-stresses-on-the-need-for-half-point-rate-hike-in-december-says-i-am-very-concerned-about-inflation/cNbg5eSR9LV).
items.score_note: Explicitly wants a larger or faster sequence of hikes starting in December.

items.speaker: Philip Jefferson
items.occasion: IMF and Central Bank of Brazil conference 'A Quarter Century of Inflation Targeting in Latin America', Brasilia: 'Monetary Policy amid Frequent and Complex Shocks'
items.quote: For the U.S. economy, my goal is to restore price stability while maintaining a solid labor market.
items.summary: Short panel remarks restating his shock framework: energy shock creates an inflation/employment tradeoff, and a stronger reaction is warranted if expectations risk becoming unanchored; the AI buildout is currently adding to demand and inflation. No comment on the December decision or the rate path.
items.score_note: Framework remarks with two-sided conditional statements and no rate-path lean; scored 0 rather than +1 because nothing is said about the next move.

items.score_note: About the framework (2% target), not the rate path, so not scored; directionally it rejects accommodating higher inflation. Article body is paywalled, so the occasion is not confirmed.

coverage_notes: All 26 listed official texts (25 speeches + Bowman's June 4 testimony) were opened and itemised; 15 have no rate-path content and are scored null. Cross-checked against the Fed's own index feeds (ne-speeches.json, ne-testimony.json, ne-press.json): no other speech, testimony or individual statement by the three in the window. FOMC statements of June 17 (12-0), July 29 (9-3: Hammack, Kashkari, Logan for a hike), September 16 (12-0) and October 28 (10-2: Cook, Hammack for a hike) were opened: none of the three dissented, so there are no dissent items. time_et for official speeches comes from the Fed index feed (ET release/delivery time), not from the speech page itself; it is null for news-sourced items. Same-day pairs from one occasion are split into prepared text and Q&A and should be deduplicated if one-per-occasion is needed: Waller 2026-09-03 (Reuters NEXT), Jefferson 2026-10-01 (Darden), Bowman 2026-10-01 (Atlantic Council), Bowman 2026-11-10 (CFR). Bowman's two 2026-09-18 items are two texts posted for the same Mansion House event. Bowman's Nov 10 remarks were repeated identically at an Unleash Prosperity Now virtual event (not itemised separately). waller20260928a.htm is dated September 29 on the page and in the index. Thin months: June (only Bowman's regulatory testimony and Waller's dollar-conference welcome), August (nothing found for any of the three; no Jackson Hole interviews located) and, for Bowman, June to September (Newsquawk on Sept 18 noted she had not commented on policy since May). Jefferson has no policy remarks between July 16 and October 1. Non-listed occasions found: Waller Reuters NEXT Q&A (Sep 3), Waller at Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi (Oct 13), Waller on CNBC (Nov 18), Bowman Atlantic Council Q&A (Oct 1), Bowman in Bangkok (Oct 14), Bowman CFR Q&A (Nov 10), Jefferson Darden Q&A (Oct 1), Jefferson on the 2% target (Nov 19). No podcast appearance or print interview (WSJ, FT, NYT) by any of the three was found. Paywalled or blocked and therefore not read in full: Bloomberg originals (used syndicated copies on National Mortgage News / American Banker, which show only the first paragraphs), Axios, CNBC's own page for the Nov 18 interview (quote taken from the Reuters report). The Jefferson Darden Q&A page blocks scripted download (HTTP 403); its quote was read through the web-fetch tool only. The Atlantic Council transcript is marked AI-generated.
